articles.title: The decline of South Africa's mining sector: Challenges and opportunities - weekendargus.co.za
articles.summary: The decline of South Africa's mining sector: Challenges and opportunities  weekendargus.co.za
articles.full_text:
A new Bureau for Economic Research (BER) document indicated that South Africa’s mining sector has been in decline in recent years but still has potential to be a force globally.
Robert Botha from BER said that the economic history of South Africa is intimately bound to the extraction of its mineral wealth.
“Despite this geological lottery, the sector faces various constraints that have prevented it from taking full advantage of successive commodity booms. Once the primary engine of the economy, the sector’s economic contribution has stagnated, allowing the notion to take hold that South African mining is a sunset sector,” Botha said.
Botha added that despite successive commodity price booms, in real terms the sector has declined since 1994. “Over this period, the sector contracted by 0.29% on average. By 2024, the sector was nearly 12% smaller than it was in 1994. The long-term performance of the South African mining sector is defined by a significant structural decline that began in the 1970s. A collapsing gold sector, once the backbone of the economy, reduced aggregate mining production volumes.”
Botha said the most profound evidence of structural failure occurred during the global "Missed Super-Cycle" (2001–2008). “While peer resource-rich nations like Australia saw mining investment and GDP surge due to Chinese industrialisation, South Africa’s mining contribution actually shrank by 1%. Research indicates that this divergence was largely driven by domestic policy transitions rather than geology.”
Botha added that the trajectory of investor confidence, as tracked by the Fraser Institute, reveals a steady descent. “South Africa transitioned from a premier investment destination in the early 2000s to a bottom-tier jurisdiction by 2024. This decline was accelerated by the policy shock era (2004–2010), followed by a crisis of confidence era (2011–2017) which was marked by labour unrest and state-led corruption.”
Botha said despite a long-term decline in real terms, the South African mining sector remains a cornerstone of the national economy. “In 2024, the industry directly contributed R442 billion, representing 6% of the nominal GDP. Beyond its direct output, the sector functions as a vital economic engine through significant multiplier effects. The Minerals Council estimates an employment multiplier of ten, meaning every direct mining job supports ten additional opportunities in other sectors.”
Botha added that the sector is the primary anchor for South Africa’s external trade balance, accounting for over 50% of all merchandise export earnings. “This trade surplus provides a critical cushion for the current account, helping to offset structural deficits caused by the importation of machinery and refined fuels.”
Botha said that between 2018 and 2024, the sector accounted for between 6.5% and 10.9% of total national revenue through corporate income tax, mining royalties, and personal income tax. “In real terms, the industry has shrunk by 11.5% since 1994, exerting a persistent drag on national GDP growth. This decline is primarily driven by the collapse of the gold sector, which saw an 84% reduction in output over this period. However, if gold production is excluded, the rest of the sector actually grew by 41%, revealing a stark divergence in sub-sector performance.”
Botha added that mining employment has steadily contracted from its 1987 peak of over 760,000 jobs to approximately 465,000 today, reflecting a disconnect between rising wages and stagnating labour productivity. “Furthermore, the sector faces a capital productivity paradox where increased fixed capital formation, which reached R159 billion in 2024, fails to translate into higher volumes due to external constraints.”
Botha said South Africa possesses one of the world's most significant mineral endowments. “The country holds the world’s largest reserves of Platinum Group Metals (PGMs) and manganese, as well as the second largest deposits of chromium, positioning it as an indispensable anchor in global industrial value chains. Despite this wealth, the sector's full potential remains largely latent: with only 9% to 14% of the country geo-mapped at a detailed 1:50,000 scale, significant discoveries likely remain untapped.”
Botha added that structurally, the industry is split between large-cap multinational majors and a vital but struggling junior mining sector. “The majors—such as Anglo American and Glencore—operate at a massive scale, focusing on brownfields exploration to extend the life of existing assets. Junior miners serve as the industry’s research-and-development arm, focusing on high-risk greenfields exploration. The long-term health of the industry depends on a functional relationship where juniors discover new deposits and majors bring them into production.”

articles.title: Philippines positions Pax Silica as manufacturing and FDI growth lever - Traders Union
articles.summary: Philippines positions Pax Silica as manufacturing and FDI growth lever  Traders Union
articles.full_text:
The Philippines is weighing Pax Silica as a long-term industrial policy path to raise manufacturing capacity and support its move beyond upper-middle-income status. The proposal is presented as a way to draw larger foreign direct investment inflows, strengthen high-value industries and reduce the risk of falling into a middle-income trap.
Highlights
- Economist Bernardo M. Villegas argues Pax Silica can leverage Philippines' manufacturing base and FDI if Luzon Economic Corridor commitments are upheld.
- Villegas projects Pax Silica could help the Philippines attract $15 billion to $20 billion in annual FDI, matching Vietnam's performance over two decades.
- Pax Silica's success depends on lifting the investment-to-GDP ratio toward 30% and implementing education and labor-market reforms to prevent remaining a low-value supplier.
Pax Silica strategy and policy rationale
As reported by BusinessWorld Online, economist Bernardo M. Villegas argues that Pax Silica could become one of the Philippines' most important industrial policy openings over the next decade if commitments under the Luzon Economic Corridor are delivered, particularly through infrastructure support and foreign direct investments.
He frames the initiative as part of a broader effort to combine stronger manufacturing, food security and better governance. While the Philippines attains upper-middle-income economy status in 2026 under World Bank standards, he says reaching high-income status over the next 20 years requires a deeper industrial base and more sustained capital formation.
Villegas contrasts that objective with the experience of several Latin American economies that reached upper-middle-income status but later stagnated under weak policy choices. He says the Philippines avoided some of those outcomes because economic institutions, including the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, have been strengthened over the past three decades and some anti-FDI policies have been corrected.
He also links Pax Silica to the country's earlier industrial policy failures. In his assessment, protectionist and inward-looking strategies after independence from the U.S. left the Philippines without a strong manufacturing base, while regional peers pursued export-oriented industrialization and gave more weight to countryside and agricultural development.
Potential industry gains and economic impact
Villegas says Pax Silica could help the Philippines move directly into Industry 4.0 activities even after missing earlier waves of industrialization. He identifies advanced semiconductor manufacturing and packaging, AI computing and data centers, electronics and advanced equipment, critical mineral processing, engineering and research, robotics and automation, and logistics as possible areas of investment.
He says the initiative could help the country attract $15 billion to $20 billion in annual FDI, a level he compares with Vietnam's performance over the past two decades. He argues that without lifting the investment-to-GDP ratio closer to the East Asian average of 30%, the Philippines is unlikely to reach high-income status within 20 years, especially as domestic savings and additional borrowing are insufficient to supply that scale of capital.
In that framework, Pax Silica could make the Philippines more attractive to global manufacturers seeking production sites within trusted country networks, provided the country offers reliable energy, efficient infrastructure, skilled labor, competitive taxation and predictable regulation. Villegas adds that the plan could generate better-paying jobs for engineers, software developers, AI specialists, technicians, researchers, data-center specialists and industrial managers.
He also says the policy raises pressure for education and labor-market reforms, echoing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s call to shift more strongly toward technical-vocational education and training. At the same time, he warns that Pax Silica risks leaving the Philippines as only a supplier of land, minerals, utilities and low-cost labor unless government, universities, TESDA and businesses build specialized training and research programs for semiconductors, automation, power systems, data-center operations, precision engineering, industrial utilities and cybersecurity.
In our earlier article on the Philippines’ planned sovereign bond pricing reforms and expected inclusion in a major emerging-market government bond index, we explained how these changes could broaden the investor base and improve liquidity for peso government securities. We also noted that cheaper funding and stronger market access do not automatically translate into factory-building and productivity gains unless they are matched by credible fiscal management and wider structural reforms—such as better infrastructure, governance, and deeper domestic capital markets that can finance business expansion.

articles.title: South Africa: Ramaphosa prepares the country for a possible exclusion from AGOA - Bénin Web TV
articles.summary: South Africa: Ramaphosa prepares the country for a possible exclusion from AGOA  Bénin Web TV
articles.full_text:
Economy
South Africa: Ramaphosa prepares the country for a possible exclusion from AGOA
The South African president has warned that a loss of U.S. trade preferences would severely impact employment. Meanwhile, Pretoria is accelerating its search for markets in China and India.
Cyril Ramaphosa urged South Africa on Monday, October 19, to prepare for a possible exclusion from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), the U.S. program that provides duty-free access for thousands of African products. The president spoke in Johannesburg during a discussion with editors and journalists organized to commemorate Black Wednesday.
The continuation of Pretoria’s participation remains uncertain despite the extension of AGOA until December 31, 2028. This renewal prolongs the law, but the eligibility of each country is still assessed individually, and several U.S. officials have called for South Africa to be excluded.
Ramaphosa indicated that his government is continuing discussions with Washington without any guarantees regarding their outcome. He stated that an exclusion would have a “devastating” effect on employment and emphasized the need to prepare the country for this possibility.
The risk primarily affects sectors oriented towards the U.S. market. The automotive and agricultural industries are among the most vulnerable, as the loss of trade preferences would increase the cost of South African exports and weaken their competitiveness against products from other countries still included in the program.
To mitigate this shock, Ramaphosa stated that he and his deputy, Paul Mashatile, are increasing their travels to open new markets. He cited the recent implementation of a zero-duty regime by China for South African products that meet origin requirements as a positive development.
India represents another focus of this diversification. New Delhi and the Southern African Customs Union, of which South Africa is a member, signed the terms of reference for negotiations towards a preferential trade agreement on August 12. The discussions will cover goods, market access, rules of origin, and customs procedures.
This strategy does not mean that Pretoria is abandoning the U.S. market. Ramaphosa stressed the importance of continuing dialogue with U.S. authorities, while efforts towards Beijing and New Delhi aim to reduce the economic impact of a potential unfavorable decision regarding South Africa’s eligibility.

articles.title: Abiy Calls for Easier Ethiopia–Kenya Border Trade as Countries Move to Expand Economic Ties - Birr Metrics
articles.summary: Abiy Calls for Easier Ethiopia–Kenya Border Trade as Countries Move to Expand Economic Ties  Birr Metrics
articles.full_text:
Prime minister urges fewer barriers for farmers and businesses as Ethiopia prepares to double electricity exports to Kenya and authorities examine a second border crossing.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (PhD) has called for easier cross-border trade between Ethiopia and Kenya, urging both governments to create greater opportunities for farmers, producers and businesses as the neighbouring economies seek to expand commercial relations through electricity exports, telecommunications investment and transport infrastructure.
Speaking during Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret on October 20, 2026, Abiy said economic cooperation between the two countries should extend beyond existing infrastructure projects to improve market access for businesses and agricultural producers operating across their shared border.
“Our farmers and producers must be able to trade more easily across our borders,” Abiy told the gathering attended by Kenyan President William Ruto.
The remarks come four months after Ethiopia issued a directive governing simplified border trade with Kenya and as Kenyan authorities assess the feasibility of establishing an additional official crossing point along the approximately 860-kilometre frontier.
Ethiopia’s Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration issued Border Trade Directive No. 1144/2026 on June 26, establishing a regulatory framework for implementing simplified trade arrangements between the two countries.
The measure forms part of efforts to facilitate legitimate small-scale commercial exchanges across the border, where informal trading networks operate alongside established customs and transport routes.
The directive predates Abiy’s latest remarks, and no additional trade agreement, tariff concession or customs regulation was announced during his speech in Eldoret.
However, the prime minister’s intervention comes as both countries pursue practical measures intended to expand commercial activity in border communities.
On September 30, Kenya’s government disclosed that a multi-agency team had begun assessing the feasibility of opening a new border crossing at Sololo-Dukale in Marsabit County.
The assessment, undertaken by the Border Control and Operations Coordination Committee, covers the suitability of the proposed crossing for customs administration, immigration procedures, security operations and cross-border trade.
Kennedy Nyaiyo, Head of Kenya’s Border Management Secretariat, said the Moyale crossing remains the only officially designated entry point along the Kenya–Ethiopia border in Marsabit County.
The proposed Sololo-Dukale crossing would provide an additional formal route for traders and residents if approved and developed.
Kenyan authorities have not announced a construction budget, opening date or final decision establishing the crossing.
Moyale currently serves as an important commercial and transport link between southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya.
The crossing connects Ethiopia’s road network with Kenya’s northern transport corridor, providing access to markets and transport infrastructure extending towards Nairobi and the Port of Mombasa.
The corridor has been developed under wider regional infrastructure initiatives intended to improve transport links between Kenya, Ethiopia and South Sudan.
For traders, the commercial significance of improved border procedures depends on several factors, including customs clearance requirements, permitted commodities, transport costs, road conditions and the availability of supporting services.
Cross-border trade involves agricultural products, livestock and other goods exchanged between businesses and communities in northern Kenya and southern Ethiopia.
The two countries also maintain formal commercial relationships in manufactured goods, agricultural products, telecommunications and electricity.
Electricity trade has become an increasingly important component of their economic relationship.
Ethiopia began supplying electricity to Kenya through the Ethiopia–Kenya high-voltage transmission interconnection in 2022, creating a direct channel for cross-border electricity sales.
The interconnection links Ethiopia’s electricity generation system with Kenya’s national grid and forms part of wider efforts to integrate electricity markets across Eastern Africa.
In September 2026, Ethiopian Electric Power announced preparations to increase exports to Kenya from 200 megawatts to 400 megawatts beginning in December.
The utility said a joint technical committee had started work on the technical requirements, including trial operations and measures needed to maintain the stability of the interconnected systems.
The planned increase would double the volume of contracted electricity supply, subject to completion of the necessary technical and operational preparations.
No new electricity supply agreement or revised export tariff was announced during Abiy’s visit to Kenya.
The electricity connection provides Ethiopia with an export market for its generation capacity while allowing Kenya to supplement its domestic power supply through imports.
Ethiopia’s power generation is dominated by hydropower, including production from major projects on the country’s river systems.
Electricity exports also provide an additional source of foreign currency earnings, although the revenue generated depends on actual electricity deliveries and the terms of the relevant power purchase agreements.
Abiy referred to the electricity connection during his speech, identifying energy cooperation as an established component of the bilateral economic relationship.
He also pointed to Safaricom’s operations in Ethiopia as an example of private-sector investment connecting the two economies.
The Kenyan telecommunications group entered Ethiopia following the award of a telecommunications licence to a consortium led by Safaricom in 2021.
Safaricom Ethiopia launched commercial mobile services in October 2022, introducing competition into a market previously dominated by state-owned Ethio Telecom.
The company has subsequently expanded its telecommunications network, customer base and mobile financial services through M-Pesa Ethiopia.
Safaricom’s Ethiopian investment represents one of the largest cross-border private-sector investments involving companies headquartered in Kenya.
Its operations also provide a commercial connection between the two markets through telecommunications infrastructure, digital services and financial technology.
During his Eldoret address, Abiy referred to the role of Safaricom and M-Pesa in expanding communications and payment services in Ethiopia.
The growth of mobile financial services in both countries forms part of a wider transition towards digital payments and financial inclusion.
However, the presence of M-Pesa in Ethiopia and Kenya does not automatically establish unrestricted cross-border money transfers between customers in the two countries. Such services are subject to licensing, foreign exchange requirements, payment regulations and the availability of authorised transfer arrangements.
The prime minister also referred to the transport corridor linking Mombasa and Hawassa, highlighting the role of roads and regional infrastructure in connecting businesses and markets.
Kenya’s Port of Mombasa provides an alternative maritime gateway in East Africa, although Ethiopia’s international merchandise trade continues to move predominantly through Djibouti.
The development of transport links through northern Kenya has formed part of regional plans to improve access to markets and reduce logistical barriers between neighbouring economies.
Infrastructure investment along these routes has included road construction, border facilities and related transport projects.
The economic benefits of these investments depend on their use by commercial operators, the competitiveness of freight services and the efficiency of customs and border administration.
The Ethiopia–Kenya relationship also operates within the broader framework of the African Continental Free Trade Area and regional integration initiatives.
Both countries are members of the African Union and participate in the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, which promotes regional cooperation in areas including economic development, infrastructure and security.
Kenya is also a member of the East African Community, while Ethiopia is not, meaning their bilateral trade is governed by a different combination of national, bilateral and continental arrangements.
For small-scale traders operating along the frontier, implementation of simplified border trade procedures could affect the documentation and clearance requirements associated with moving eligible goods.
The Ethiopian directive issued in June provides a regulatory basis for those arrangements, but the scale of trade conducted under the new framework has not been publicly quantified in the sources reviewed.
No official figures were announced during Abiy’s speech showing how many traders have used the directive, the value of goods cleared under it or changes in border-processing times.
Similarly, Kenya’s proposed Sololo-Dukale crossing remains under feasibility assessment rather than construction or operation.
The latest remarks therefore come against a backdrop of existing regulatory and infrastructure measures rather than the announcement of a new bilateral trade agreement.
Alongside commercial cooperation, Abiy called for greater movement of people between the two countries, including travel, cultural exchanges and educational opportunities.
“Let more of our people visit each other’s countries, discover our cultures, and learn together,” he said.
The prime minister’s remarks placed farmers, producers and private businesses at the centre of his appeal for stronger bilateral economic relations.

articles.summary: ​Addis–Sharjah business forum to bring UAE investors to Ethiopia  Capital Newspaper
articles.full_text:
Ethiopia is set to host the Addis–Sharjah Business Forum this week, bringing together investors and enterprises from Sharjah, United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Ethiopian businesses to bolster trade relations, promote cross-border investment, and establish new market linkages.
The forum is jointly organized by the Addis Ababa Chamber of Commerce and Sectoral Associations (Addis Chamber), Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the UAE Embassy in Ethiopia, and the Ethiopian Embassy in the UAE.
The business-to-business (B2B) platform will connect Ethiopian manufacturers, service providers, exporters, and importers directly with Sharjah-based executives and investors operating across diverse economic sectors. The sessions aim to facilitate commercial partnerships, unlock investment opportunities, and expand international market access for participating businesses while enhancing local companies’ global competitiveness.
Organizers confirmed that the Addis Chamber has finalized preparations to support local participants spanning key growth sectors, including manufacturing, agriculture, services, and trade.
A central highlight of the event will be the official signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Addis Chamber and the Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The agreement aims to solidify institutional cooperation in trade and investment promotion while facilitating closer ties between the business communities of both regions.
The Addis Chamber continues to lead efforts to attract foreign direct investment to Ethiopia—particularly Addis Ababa—by organizing trade delegations, facilitating international commercial partnerships, and opening global market access channels for local enterprises.
The forum reflects rapidly expanding economic ties between Ethiopia and the UAE. Figures cited by event organizers indicate that bilateral trade surpassed $6 billion in 2025, underlining the strategic value of deepening bilateral commercial collaboration.

articles.title: EU Approves Sh462 Billion for Tanzania, Redirects Support to Private Sector in Line with Global Gateway and Dira 2050 - The Chanzo
articles.summary: EU Approves Sh462 Billion for Tanzania, Redirects Support to Private Sector in Line with Global Gateway and Dira 2050  The Chanzo
articles.full_text:
Dar es Salaam — The European Union has approved a €156 million, equivalent to Sh462.8 billion, package for Tanzania, but the decision does not restore direct EU budget support to the government.
Instead, the Commission’s action plan says support will be delivered through other partners and modalities after the political and human-rights deterioration surrounding the October 2025 election.
That distinction is central to the ongoing debate in Tanzania following reports, including by the government-owned Daily News newspaper, that the funding has been “unlocked” after a delay.
A European Commission financing decision makes the full allocation available for implementation, but it does not mean that the money has already been transferred or spent.
The Commission signed the decision on July 24, 2026, approving an Annual Action Plan for 2026, not 2025 as stated in some media reports. It sets a maximum EU contribution of €156 million and authorises three actions: €129 million for mineral and agricultural value chains, €20 million for a digital economy and connectivity initiative, and €7 million for a cooperation facility.
The EU Delegation told The Chanzo that the Daily News information was correct and that, “in line with the Global Gateway strategy and DIRA 2050, the funds will be channelled through and benefit the private sector.” It added: “This will be mutually beneficial for both Tanzanian and EU interests.”
The Delegation’s response, however, did not set out the amounts, final implementing partners or schedule for contracts and payments. But it said it could clarify those questions as well, but it may require “additional time for internal consultations.”
The private-sector emphasis is not new in itself. Global Gateway, the EU’s investment strategy launched before the current dispute, is expressly designed to mobilise private investment in sectors such as digital, energy and transport while creating opportunities for European companies.
In 2024, the EU used that model in Tanzania by blending a €15 million grant with up to €350 million in European Investment Bank credit lines to local banks for small and medium-sized businesses. The EIB said the grant was intended partly to reduce the risk to banks of lending to firms, including women-led and blue-economy enterprises.
What’s new
What is new is the action plan’s stated response to the political crisis. Its three action documents say the partnership has been affected by deterioration in human rights, democracy and the rule of law, as well as violence during and after the Oct. 29, 2025 election, and describe a “shift in the nature of EU cooperation.”
“Whilst the EU will maintain support for the Tanzanian population, civil society and the private sector, it will do so through modalities that avoid the use of government systems,” says the €129 million value-chain action document.
The same document says ongoing budget-support programmes have been discontinued and that the EU will not enter new ones “in the foreseeable future.” It says future depth and scope of the partnership will increasingly depend on progress by Tanzanian authorities in restoring respect for human rights and the rule of law.
That places the Delegation’s reference to private-sector channels in context. It is consistent with Global Gateway and with the 2026 action plan, but it does not amount to a simple continuation of the previous relationship: the plan uses private-sector and other non-government routes as a safeguard against directing funds through government systems.
Nor is all of the €156 million a direct private-sector transfer. The value-chain action includes grants, Commission procurement, indirect management, contributions to the African Investment Platform and budgetary guarantees; it is designed to support critical-minerals processing, agricultural value chains, investment climate reforms and local value addition.
The TANTECH action, for instance, supports digital infrastructure, e-commerce, e-payments, innovation and regional digital trade. The €7 million cooperation facility is to finance technical assistance, investment studies, business missions, aviation-safety support and activities designed to prepare Global Gateway investments.
The package therefore combines development aims with stated European commercial interests. The value-chain document refers to investments that connect Tanzanian mineral and agricultural production to European industries and markets, while the cooperation facility says it will help prepare and de-risk investments aligned with EU economic interests.
The approval followed a procedural dispute without resolving the political arguments that produced it. On June 18, the European Parliament objected to the Commission’s draft decision, citing human-rights and accountability concerns and calling for a new proposal; its record says the revised proposal kept broadly the same actions and amount but moved mainly to indirect management rather than direct budget support.

articles.title: Critical minerals: Why mining communities may suffer the fate of Niger Delta - The Sun Nigeria
articles.summary: Critical minerals: Why mining communities may suffer the fate of Niger Delta  The Sun Nigeria
articles.full_text:
As Nigerians await the report of the panel set up to investigate the circumstances that led to the avoidable death of 37 artisanal miners in Niger State, it has become imperative to examine the desperation for critical minerals by non-states actors and countries like China, EU, and the US. In doing so, it is also pertinent to understand why the minerals are “critical.” A publication of the Belfer Centre for Science and International Affairs reveals the three conditions stipulated by the U.S. Energy Act of 2020 that make a mineral to be termed critical. One, the mineral has to be “essential to economic or national security.” Two, “its supply chain is vulnerable to disruption,” and three, “it performs a function in manufacturing that cannot be replaced without serious consequences, whether higher costs for key technologies, slower deployment of clean energy, or risks to defense and communications systems.”
There is another dimension that further underlines the critical element. The geopolitics of where the mineral is mined can make it critical especially, “if it is refined or processed elsewhere, particularly by a strategic rival. An example of this is China’s dominance in rare earth refining,” the Belfer Center noted. Hence, China’s likelihood of withholding supply to gain advantage is a cause for worry.
Some of these critical minerals which are inextricably connected to global transition to clean energy, production of national defense gadgetsn and artificial intelligence data storage, include copper, cobalt, lithium, manganese, graphite, nickel, rare earth elements and platinum group metals (PGMs). And to follow the momentum, advanced nations continue to update their lists of critical minerals based on technological discoveries and growing appetite for them. Already, estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA) as captured in Jordy Lee Calderon’s article in Milken Institute Review made a projection that the world “will require six times more mineral inputs for renewable technologies in 2040 than today,” just as the “Demand for lithium to manufacture rechargeable electricity storage, for example, is expected to increase at least 20-fold.”
In terms of global distribution, the highest reserves of critical minerals are unevenly spread across the leading nations of China, Australia, the Lithium Triangle region – (Chile, Argentina and Bolivia), Indonesia, as well as African countries like the Democratic of Congo (DRC), South Africa, Gabon, and Guinea. There are other countries in Africa including Nigeria that have significant deposits of critical minerals, but DRC alone has almost 75% of global cobalt reserves.
Meanwhile, with roughly 30% of global reserves of critical minerals, Africa is at the centre of strategic engagements for global supply, but unfortunately, the continent lacks the technical and technological capabilities to refine the minerals locally.
What is therefore witnessed in the continent is mostly raw extraction for exports by artisanal miners, factions and fractions of criminal cartels of the elites, as well as some powerful officials in government who exploit the weak regulatory environment to rip off their countries.
As such, the continent has inadvertently turned into battlegrounds for all manner of indigenous and external interests, with the mining sector morphing into a new rent-seeking frontier in Africa.
The 80% control of critical minerals processing and refining by China has also awoken the U.
S.
from passivity.
The irony, according to Calderon, is that it was the U.
S.
that “invented the complex industrial processes used for separating rare earth elements decades ago, then ceded production to China.
” For years, the U.
S.
and some other industrialized nations looked down on mining and metals industry, and China dominated the space.
But lately, the U.
S.
is poised to square up to China by extending its tentacles to African critical minerals sector.
The U.
S.
and E.
U.
have brokered deals to secure supplies from Africa.
And with Chinese companies already operating in some regions in Africa, including Nigeria, the battle may not be in the interest of the continent if they fail to act together.

The major challenge is that the mining sector in Africa is not strongly regulated amid the “new scramble”. Nigeria is still playing politics by pampering the big illegal miners who became billionaires overnight without verifiable economic production. Beyond that, Abraham Nunbogu and Kaveh Madani of Institute for Water, Environment and Health, United Nations University have raised concerns about creating “sacrifice zones” with the enormous amounts of water needed for minerals extraction and the health hazards in host communities in Africa and South America. They noted that, “In 2024 alone, global lithium production required an estimated 456 billion litres of water. That is equivalent to the annual domestic water needs of roughly 62 million people in sub‑Saharan Africa. At the same time, much of the world is facing water bankruptcy, meaning people and industries are using more fresh water than nature can replenish, leading to irrecoverable ecosystem damages.”
Besides, the communities close to the extraction sites have reportedly suffered “skin diseases, gastrointestinal illnesses, reproductive health problems and chronic health conditions associated with long‑term exposure to heavy metals in polluted water and soil…Evidence from mining regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is particularly stark. Studies document high rates of miscarriages, congenital malformations and infant mortality among populations exposed to environments contaminated with cobalt and other metals,” as noted by Nunbogu and Madani. The mining communities in Nigeria are also having their sad tales.
Indeed, Nigeria and other African nations are not doing enough to stop industrialized nations from eating their lunch. And if care is not taken, the continent will relapse into another round of “resource curse.” Efforts should be made to ensure that the resource wealth is used in a sustainable manner by negotiating as a team under a continental platform instead of doing it by individual countries. Agreements should prioritise skills development, local content, and a clear-cut plan for closure of mining sites after exploration. Nigeria should understudy how Norway made its hydrocarbon resources work for the present and future generations. Let Nigeria avoid another environmental despoilation occasioned by mining without responsibility like the Niger Delta.

articles.title: DARYL SWANEPOEL | Defend Agoa, but let’s resist alarmism - Business Day
articles.summary: DARYL SWANEPOEL | Defend Agoa, but let’s resist alarmism  Business Day
articles.full_text:
South Africa should do everything reasonably within its power to retain the benefits of the African Growth & Opportunity Act (Agoa) and repair its strained relationship with the US. Our economy needs stronger growth, investment and employment. We should expand trade with America while growing our other markets.
However, with an Agoa eligibility announcement expected within the next few weeks we must also consider what happens if diplomacy fails. Preparing for that possibility is responsible economic management. It requires neither indifference towards Agoa nor an invitation to Washington to withdraw it. It requires an honest assessment of the consequences.
That assessment is becoming obscured by alarmist rhetoric. Of late a number of organisations have portrayed the situation as an emergency, citing up to 250,000 jobs partially or fully dependent on Agoa and more than 500,000 associated with US trade. Their policy proposals have reinforced the sense of urgency surrounding the approaching decision.
Concern for those workers is legitimate. But employment associated with trade is not the same as employment that would disappear if a particular preference were withdrawn. The distinction is fundamental. Without it, large employment figures can create an impression of impending national economic disaster without establishing the likelihood or scale of the losses.
We should ask what exclusion would change. Which products would attract additional duties? How much would those duties rise? Which exports would remain competitive? What could be sold elsewhere? These questions matter more than the repeated presentation of the entire trading relationship as though it were about to vanish.
Our preliminary analysis of a South African Revenue Service (Sars) extract places South African merchandise exports to the US in 2025 at about R148bn. Matching identifiable mineral products against the September 2025 reciprocal tariff exemption schedule accounts for about R76bn. Complete motor vehicles account for another R17bn. Deducting these categories leaves some R55bn.
For perspective, that remainder represents about 2.7% of South Africa’s global merchandise exports and 0.73% of nominal GDP in 2025. Sars reported preliminary global merchandise exports of about R2.08-trillion, while Stats SA placed nominal GDP at about R7.6-trillion.
A fuller reconciliation with US import statistics, particularly the classification of additional gold-related imports, could reveal a smaller remaining share of exports after these deductions. The preliminary calculation may therefore overstate that share, though this requires confirmation.
These are measures of scale, not estimates of economic loss. Nor is the remainder a definitive measure of Agoa exposure. Exemption from reciprocal tariffs and exemption from ordinary customs duties under Agoa are different arrangements. Some product classifications require further examination. The calculation nevertheless illustrates why the composition of our exports deserves attention.
Motor vehicles provide a useful example. Covered passenger cars already face an additional 25% automotive tariff. Losing an Agoa preference could add the ordinary passenger-car duty of 2.5%, taking the combined rate to 27.5%. That additional cost matters, but exclusion would not suddenly create the entire new tariff burden confronting the industry. Other vehicle classifications carry different ordinary duties.
Critical minerals must also be considered within America’s strategic interests. Washington explicitly seeks diversified supplies and reduced dependence on adversarial countries, as its January 14 White House fact sheet confirms. Continued access to important South African minerals serves that objective. There are therefore sound reasons to expect favourable treatment for key mineral products to remain attractive to the US, despite diplomatic tensions.
This is an expectation, not an assurance. American policy also seeks to strengthen domestic production and leaves room for tariffs and minimum import prices. South Africa should negotiate actively around these shared supply interests, rather than assume either permanent protection or inevitable exclusion.
Even where additional duties arise, exports do not automatically cease. Buyers may continue purchasing South African products. Costs may be shared through lower exporter margins, importer adjustments and higher consumer prices. Some businesses will find alternative customers. Others will struggle. The outcome depends on competitiveness and commercial responses, rather than simply equalising the value of the exports concerned.
Agoa is a unilateral preference requiring renewal and continued eligibility. South Africa cannot confidently build its economic future around its indefinite continuation.
Agriculture demonstrates the importance of this distinction. Global agricultural exports increased from about $13.7bn in 2024 to $15.1bn in 2025. Agricultural exports to the US were $504m in 2025, down about 3%. This modest decline occurred despite the additional 30% reciprocal tariff imposed on non-exempt South African products from August 7 2025, including those qualifying for duty-free access under Agoa. However, the annual figures capture only about five months of exposure to that higher tariff.
Calculated from these rounded figures, the increase in agricultural exports to markets outside the US was about $1.42bn ― about 2.7 times the previous year’s entire agricultural exports to America. The department of agriculture reported that growth elsewhere more than offset the US losses.
That does not mean every affected farmer found an equally profitable replacement market or that all the growth resulted from redirecting US orders. It does show that diversification can cushion losses. For producers facing a largely fixed harvest in the short term, access to alternative buyers can preserve sales, though prices and margins may differ.
Our objective should be to grow both American and other markets. Agricultural resilience is evidence of our capacity to adapt, not a reason to relinquish valuable customers.
Independent research corroborates the case for proportion. A November 2023 Brookings study estimated that losing Agoa alone would reduce South Africa’s exports to the US by about 2.7% and the national GDP by about 0.06%. Its model allowed for some trade diversion towards other destinations.
The study predates the additional US automotive tariffs introduced in April 2025. Those tariffs already form part of the trading environment and their effects should be incorporated into forecasts that account for the present tariff regime. The relevant question is therefore the further impact of losing Agoa preferences, without counting the existing automotive tariff shock again.
Brookings’ estimates cannot be applied mechanically to today’s circumstances, but they provide corroborating evidence that the loss of Agoa alone need not produce dramatic, immediate economy-wide consequences. But the study does not capture potential investment and confidence effects.
The longer-term question also deserves attention. Agoa is a unilateral preference requiring renewal and continued eligibility. South Africa cannot confidently build its economic future around its indefinite continuation.
In my discussions with US policymakers and legislators since 2015, possible “graduation” was already a recurring theme. Contemporary reporting confirms that some congressional factions regarded South Africa as sufficiently developed to move towards more reciprocal trading arrangements.
Upper-middle-income status did not legally disqualify us, but our relative development supplied a political argument for graduation. The uncertainty therefore predates today’s diplomatic dispute.
Preserving Agoa and preparing for life beyond it are compatible responsibilities. We should pursue constructive diplomacy, protect existing commercial relationships, develop more durable trade arrangements and assist businesses most exposed to additional duties.
None of this discounts the workers and communities for whom even a modest national loss could be devastating. Targeted support requires identifying those risks accurately. Alarmism offers little help in doing so.
South Africa should defend Agoa because it is valuable. We should also assess possible exclusion with evidence and proportion. A clear understanding of our vulnerabilities and capacity to adapt will strengthen our decisions while we continue working for the outcome we want: a healthier relationship with the US and expanding trade with it.
• Swanepoel is CEO of the Inclusive Society Institute.

Uganda’s exports to the European Union have quadrupled over the past decade, reaching €1.8 billion (Shs 8.4tn) in 2025, according to EU Ambassador Jan Sadek, as the private sector calls for increased processing of locally produced goods to capture greater value from the expanding trade relationship.
Sadek said Uganda’s exports to the EU had risen from €420 million in 2015 to €1.8 billion in 2025, highlighting the growth of commercial ties between the two sides as they mark 50 years of partnership.
“Uganda’s exports to the European Union has quadrupled, ladies and gentlemen, from 420 million euros in 2015 to 1.8 billion euros in 2025,” Sadek said at the Uganda-EU Business Forum.
He said the EU’s Everything But Arms arrangement gives Uganda duty-free and quota-free access to the European market for eligible products, providing an opportunity for Ugandan businesses to expand their exports.
Sadek said the partnership was important at a time of growing global economic uncertainty and pressure on supply chains, arguing that reliable commercial relationships were increasingly important for countries and businesses.
“Europe’s message to Uganda is simple. You can rely on us,” he said.
PSFU Deputy Chair Sarah Kagingo said Uganda needed to build on its export performance by processing more of what it produces instead of relying on the sale of lower-value products.
“The next steps should be to build on this performance by processing more of what we produce and supplying higher value products to the European market,” Kagingo said.
She said stronger trade relations should create opportunities for local enterprises to expand production, improve competitiveness and employ more Ugandans.
Kagingo cited European Commission figures showing that bilateral trade in goods between Uganda and the EU reached approximately €2.35 billion in 2025. She said Uganda exported €1.64 billion worth of goods to the bloc and imported €713 million, giving the country a trade surplus of €923 million.
Kagingo said the private sector wanted stronger commercial relations to translate into increased production and higher-value exports, with investment helping Ugandan businesses compete in international markets.
Energy and Mineral Development Minister, Dr. Monica Musenero, who represented Vice President Jessica Alupo at the forum, urged European businesses to consider Uganda not only as an export destination but also as a base for manufacturing, value addition and expansion into regional markets.
She said Uganda’s strategic position within the East African Community and its access to the wider African market through the African Continental Free Trade Area offered opportunities for investors seeking to serve markets beyond Uganda.
Musenero said government remained committed to strengthening the investment climate through infrastructure development, regulatory improvements and public-private partnerships.
She also called on European partners to support greater value addition in agriculture, minerals and renewable energy technologies, arguing that stronger commercial links should generate sustainable employment and improve Uganda’s competitiveness.
The minister said cooperation should extend beyond the movement of goods and capital to include technology transfer, skills development, research, innovation and greater local participation in production and supply chains.
Sadek said the EU was also Uganda’s leading investment partner, citing approximately €2.2 billion in European foreign direct investment during the previous year. He said this represented around 79% of all foreign direct investment in Uganda.
He said the economic relationship was reflected in business activity and livelihoods, including factories, farms, salaries and employment.
The Uganda-EU Business Forum is focused on deepening commercial ties as the two sides mark five decades of relations, with participants seeking to identify investment opportunities that can expand trade, strengthen production and support economic growth.

articles.title: Ramaphosa tells South Africa to prepare for loss of US-Africa trade deal - France 24
articles.summary: Ramaphosa tells South Africa to prepare for loss of US-Africa trade deal  France 24
articles.full_text:
Johannesburg (AFP) – South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Monday the country should "prepare" for the possibility of being removed from Washington's duty-free trade programme for Africa, as ties between the two nations continue to fray.
Issued on:
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which grants eligible sub-Saharan African countries preferential access to the US market, has been renewed until the end of 2028.
South Africa is the scheme's largest beneficiary but its eligibility has come under scrutiny as Washington steps up criticism of Pretoria, including false allegations of discrimination against white Afrikaners that South Africa rejects.
"Congress has decided that we should be kept in AGOA. What now remains is the executive," Ramaphosa said, referring to the pact now needing President Donald Trump's signature after approval by Congress.
"And by the way, so that I prepare our people for this, if we ever have a choice, we are not the first and only country to be taken out of AGOA. And I believe we will not be the last," he said in response to a question from an AFP journalist during a briefing.
Bilateral ties have deteriorated since Trump took office, with Washington cutting aid, expelling South Africa's ambassador and berating Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide".
Washington in mid-September announced restrictions on visas for South Africans who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa" -- all issues that are disputed between the two countries.
Last year, the United States launched a programme to resettle white Afrikaners who say they face persecution and violent crime in South Africa.
By September 30, the United States had admitted 16,287 South Africans under the programme over the preceding year. They were the only people granted refugee status by Washington during that period, apart from five Afghans.
'Devastating' impact
The US president reviews countries' eligibility for AGOA annually.
Any removal requires 60 days' notice to Congress and the country concerned. To take effect on January 1, an exclusion must be announced by November 2.
Former president Joe Biden declared the Central African Republic, Gabon, Niger and Uganda ineligible on October 30, 2023, with the exclusions taking effect on January 1, 2024.
South Africa is going to look for alternative markets to minimise the impacts of such an exclusion, Ramaphosa said.
"I need as president to prepare us if it ever happens. So we should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world," he said, conceding that the impacts would nonetheless be "devastating".
Within AGOA, Washington exempts South African cars from customs duties.
After precious metals, cars are the country's second-biggest export earner to the United States, according to the South African tax authorities.
In 2025, the automobile employers' organisation Naamsa said 86,000 jobs were directly tied to the accord at car manufacturers, a number that increases to 125,000 when including their sub-contractors.

articles.title: Zimbabwe moves up Africa’s largest economy rankings at $65.9 billion, but heavy US dollar reliance has not helped it match Tanzania’s growth - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Zimbabwe moves up Africa’s largest economy rankings at $65.9 billion, but heavy US dollar reliance has not helped it match Tanzania’s growth  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Zimbabwe is projected to be Africa’s 14th largest economy in 2026 with a GDP of $65.92 billion, supported by agriculture and mining recovery.
- Zimbabwe’s economic growth is forecast at 5% for 2026, lower than Tanzania’s projected 5.9%, due in part to different monetary policies.
- Zimbabwe continues to face persistent challenges from high inflation, currency volatility, and significant debt arrears, restricting access to international finance.
- Tanzania, in contrast, has strengthened the use of its national currency, seen stronger GDP growth, and diversified through major energy and infrastructure investments.
According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook, Zimbabwe ranks 14th among Africa’s largest economies, ahead of Cameroon at $64.81 billion and Tunisia at $62.74 billion.
The latest position marks an improvement from earlier IMF estimates, which placed the country 17th in 2025 with GDP of $51.22 billion. In April 2026, the Fund ranked it 16th at $56.71 billion, before revising its projections in October.
The southern African economy is expected to grow by 5% in 2026, following an estimated 8.3% expansion in 2025, supported by favourable gold prices, recovering agricultural production and remittance inflows.
Despite these gains, Zimbabwe trails Tanzania, whose economy is projected at $96.18 billion, $30.26 billion larger, with growth forecast at 5.9% in 2026.
The two countries also differ in currency policy, with Zimbabwe heavily reliant on the US dollar while Tanzania has strengthened the use of its national currency in domestic transactions.
Zimbabwe's recovery highlights currency challenges
Years of high inflation, currency depreciation and repeated monetary reforms have weakened confidence in Zimbabwe's local currency, driving widespread use of the US dollar.
In April 2024, the government introduced the Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG) to replace its previous currency and restore monetary stability.
Despite the reform, the US dollar remains dominant, accounting for about two-thirds of payments by value in the national payment system, according to the IMF's May 2026 assessment.
The currency transition also affected major businesses, including Econet Wireless Zimbabwe, founded by billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, which adjusted its payment systems to accommodate the ZiG.
While continued reliance on the US dollar has helped households and businesses protect their finances against local currency depreciation, it has limited the central bank's control over monetary policy.
In response, authorities tightened monetary measures to stabilise prices and exchange rates, with annual ZiG inflation reaching 3.7% in September 2026, up from 2.9% in August, according to the Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency.
The IMF acknowledged improvements in economic stability in its August assessment but called for continued fiscal discipline and reforms to strengthen confidence in the financial system.
Despite these gains, Zimbabwe's history of currency instability complicates comparisons of its economic performance with other African countries.
Nominal GDP expressed in US dollars is influenced by exchange rates and national accounting methods, meaning currency movements can change international rankings without corresponding changes in production.
This is particularly relevant to Zimbabwe, whose national accounts were redenominated following the introduction of the ZiG in 2024, according to the IMF's October 2026 database.
Consequently, the country's projected $65.92 billion GDP reflects its economic output in dollar terms rather than providing a direct measure of monetary stability or living standards.
Tanzania offers a different economic picture
Tanzania, meanwhile, has pursued a different approach to currency management, taking steps to strengthen the use of the Tanzanian shilling in domestic transactions.
In March 2025, the government introduced regulations requiring businesses to price goods and services and accept payments in shillings, subject to specified exceptions.
Alongside these measures, agriculture, construction, mining, tourism and infrastructure investment have supported economic growth.
The country is also pursuing a proposed $42 billion liquefied natural gas project involving international energy companies, although a final investment decision remains pending.
Tanzania's faster projected growth reflects these broader economic activities and investment trends rather than currency policy alone. Both countries remain exposed to exchange rate pressures and external economic risks.

articles.title: What does owning a foreign mine actually buy India? - The Daily Brief by Zerodha
articles.summary: What does owning a foreign mine actually buy India?  The Daily Brief by Zerodha
articles.full_text:
Our goal with The Daily Brief is to simplify the biggest stories in the Indian markets and help you understand what they mean. We won’t just tell you what happened; we’ll tell you why and how too. We do this show in both formats: video and audio. This piece curates the stories that we talk about.
You can listen to the podcast on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or wherever you get your podcasts and watch the videos on YouTube. You can also watch The Daily Brief in Hindi.
Just a quick heads-up before we dive in. The Jio Platforms IPO opened today. We wrote about it then, and you can read the full story here.
In today’s edition of The Daily Brief:
1. What does owning a foreign mine actually buy India?
To secure critical industrial raw materials like coking coal, copper, and lithium, India has launched a ₹34,300-crore National Critical Mineral Mission targeting 50 overseas mines by 2031. However, recent disputes over Tata Chemicals’ soda ash mine in Kenya and operational bottlenecks in Mozambique show that owning foreign mines acts primarily as a price hedge and output claim rather than guaranteeing discounted minerals, while failing to overcome host-nation export bans or China’s overwhelming dominance in global mineral refining.
2. Why would rivals agree on when to compete?
Biocon recently settled a global patent dispute with Genentech over its breast cancer biosimilar, Pebrilzo, agreeing to delay its lucrative US market entry until late 2028. While US patent rules allow originator firms to protect drugs using secondary process and dosing patents, European markets open faster as patients shift to newer treatments. In contrast, Indian patent law places a higher burden of proof on originators, enabling domestic drugmakers to challenge secondary patents and launch affordable biosimilars sooner.
What does owning a foreign mine actually buy India?
In early September, Kenya’s President William Ruto told Tata Chemicals to leave the country.
He was talking about Magadi, a soda ash operation on the shores of a Kenyan lake that has run since 1911, and that Tata Chemicals has owned since 2005. Soda ash, in case you’re wondering, is a key ingredient in glass, detergents and a host of everyday products.
This was no small project. Magadi can produce around 350,000 tonnes of soda ash a year, sold to buyers across India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa. Yet by the time Ruto spoke, shipments had already been halted for weeks, while the government reviewed whether Tata was following local rules. Tata says it is fully compliant, and is waiting for a government panel’s decision, with a High Court hearing due in November.
But Ruto’s complaint wasn’t really about paperwork. It was about what Kenya gets out of the mine. He wanted to bring in new investors to build a glass factory and a chemicals plant in Kenya.
We came across this story while trying to make sense of a bigger push. India, through both its government and its companies, is trying to secure minerals abroad, and owning foreign mines is a big part of that plan. Magadi made us ask a simple question: what does owning a mine actually get you?
To answer that, it helps to start at the other end. A steel mill or a battery maker doesn’t want a mine for its own sake. It needs three things. It needs the right material, in a form its plant can actually use. It needs that material to arrive reliably, without anyone else being able to switch it off. And it needs a price it can plan around. That’s the story we wanted to pursue today.
Why is India looking abroad at all?
It isn’t because India lacks minerals underground. From what we can tell, it’s because what lies underground often isn’t what our factories need. Each mineral has its own story.
Take coal. India has over 400 billion tonnes of coal resources.
Most of that, though, is the kind burnt in power plants. Steelmakers need coking coal, which is heated without oxygen to make coke, the carbon-rich fuel that runs a blast furnace. And much of India’s coking coal carries too much ash. Washing can bring that ash down to around 16–18%, but a significant portion of the coal is lost in the process, and what’s left is still well short of the low-ash coal steelmakers prefer. So India imported around 66 million tonnes of coking coal in FY26.
Copper has a different problem. India has 1.66 billion tonnes of copper ore resources, but only about 9.87% of these resources are classified as economically mineable. The rest is too poor in quality, or too costly to dig out. So India’s smelters import about 85% of the copper concentrate they use. Concentrate is ore that has already been crushed and processed to raise its copper content, ready to be smelted into metal.
Lithium is further behind still. India has identified lithium deposits in Jammu and Kashmir, but when the government put the block up for auction, it drew no bids, and the auction was cancelled.
That’s three minerals with three different gaps, but they end in the same place: the material Indian industry needs isn’t coming out of Indian ground in the form, or the volume, it needs.
That’s the gap the government now wants to fill from abroad. In January 2025, it approved the National Critical Mineral Mission, a ₹34,300-crore plan spread over seven years, which includes a target of securing 50 overseas mines by 2030–31. And since finding a mine worth owning is expensive and uncertain, in July 2026, it introduced a scheme to share some of those costs. It offers up to ₹100 crore for early exploration, and up to ₹300 crore for drilling to find out how much mineral a deposit actually holds.
The scheme’s fine print is revealing. Companies that take this money must agree to supply a share of whatever they find to Indian buyers, but at prices comparable to international rates. In other words, the government isn’t trying to get India cheaper minerals. It’s trying to get India access. That tells us a fair bit about what “security” means in official thinking.
The rest of the state machinery is moving too. The Steel Ministry has reportedly asked SAIL and NMDC to scout for mines abroad, both have set up units in GIFT City to finance such deals. The Mines Ministry also has placed officials in Indian embassies in 13 mineral-rich countries to help companies deal with local rules.
India isn’t alone in this race. The US has been spending heavily on its own supplies, including a $12 billion strategic minerals stockpile under President Trump, and another $3 billion announced in August 2026 for mineral and battery projects
One distinction is worth making before we go further. Not every Indian-owned mine abroad is about India’s supply. Vedanta, for instance, is investing nearly $600 million to double its South African zinc capacity to 500,000 tonnes a year. But zinc is a metal India largely produces at home, with Hindustan Zinc alone holding about 77% of the domestic market. That’s a sensible commercial bet, but it isn’t a supply-security play.
Why not just sign long-term contracts?
Before asking what owning a mine buys, it’s worth asking whether you need to own one at all. The simplest route to steady supply is to sign long-term agreements with several suppliers, across several countries. There’s no mine to buy and no foreign regulator to manage, and if one supplier falters, you lean on another.
This works better than one might expect. Copper concentrate has been scarce worldwide since 2024, yet Hindalco says it isn’t facing supply problems, because of its long-standing supplier relationships. Relationships, it seems, are a form of security in their own right.
But a contract has a hard limit. It’s a promise from a seller, and the seller’s government can override it. Countries have been introducing export restrictions on cobalt, lithium, graphite, rare earths, bauxite, manganese and more.
When that happens, a contract is only as good as the export licence behind it. And a contract does nothing for price, since you pay whatever the market charges. So contracts secure supply in normal times, and normal times aren’t when anyone worries about supply. That, presumably, is why companies and governments go a step further and buy into the mine itself.
So what does owning a mine actually get you?
Three Indian bets, each at a different stage, give us a reasonable picture.
The earliest is KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India Ltd), a joint venture of three public-sector companies set up to secure minerals abroad. In January 2024, it signed an agreement with Argentina’s Catamarca province to explore five areas for lithium. But what it holds is a licence to search, not a mine. By February 2026, it had only surveyed the surface, without drilling underground, and in August, Parliament was told that KABIL had spent just 10% of its $25 million five-year budget. Exploration is also a gamble. Coal India learnt this in Mozambique, where it spent around $80 million exploring two coal blocks from 2009, only to find them commercially unviable and surrender them. At this stage, ownership buys a lottery ticket and a long wait.
Further along is Benga, a coking coal mine in Mozambique controlled by ICVL, a joint venture of Indian public-sector companies formed to secure coking coal. The mine has 236 million tonnes of mineable coal, which is washed down to 10–13.5% ash so that it suits Indian steelmakers like SAIL, NMDC and RINL. But every tonne travels 15 km by truck and around 590 km by train to port before it’s shipped, on a rail system that was reported to handle only about six million tonnes a year.
Two things about Benga stood out to us. First, owning it didn’t keep it running. In 2015, when coking coal prices crashed to around $80 a tonne, ICVL halted production because the mine had become financially unviable. A mine you own still answers to the market. Second, even its owners buy its coal through a contract. SAIL sought approval for a long-term supply agreement with Benga’s operating company, alongside plans to more than double output to a

KIDF delegation engages investors and financial institutions during the Milken Institute Asia Summit.
A delegation from the Kazakhstan Investment Development Fund (KIDF) participated in the 13th Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore from 7 to 9 October 2026 to explore investment opportunities and develop partnerships with international investors. Supported by the Embassy of Kazakhstan in Singapore, the delegation engaged with financial institutions, investment funds and companies to discuss foreign direct investment and co-investment opportunities in Kazakhstan.
The delegation was led by Mr. Zhussup Yeralin, Chairman of the Management Board of KIDF, and included Mr. Turar Baissarinov, Deputy Chairman of the Management Board, and Mr. Aidyn Sadykzhan, Director of the Partnerships Department.
During the summit, Mr. Yeralin participated as a speaker in a session entitled “The Eurasian Economic Corridor: The New Geography of Global Trade Connectivity”. The discussion addressed emerging trade routes, regional connectivity and Eurasia’s role in global economic integration.
The delegation also held engagements with international investors, financial institutions, investment funds and leading companies based in Singapore. These discussions focused on attracting foreign direct investment into Kazakhstan, developing co-investment mechanisms and establishing long-term strategic partnerships in priority sectors of the country’s economy.
KIDF serves as an investment platform supporting major projects in Kazakhstan. It offers foreign partners opportunities for co-investment and minority equity participation, alongside assistance in navigating the country’s local investment environment. Through these arrangements, the fund facilitates engagement between international investors and investment projects in Kazakhstan.

The delegation’s participation reflected Kazakhstan’s engagement with Singapore-based investors and financial institutions to explore potential investment partnerships and support the development of economic ties between the two countries.

articles.title: China exits key Sri Lankan port project, abandons $392 million deal - Organiser Weekly
articles.summary: China exits key Sri Lankan port project, abandons $392 million deal  Organiser Weekly
articles.full_text:
A Chinese state-owned company has withdrawn from a proposed $392 million joint venture to develop a major logistics hub at Colombo Port, Sri Lanka’s principal seaport, prompting the Sri Lankan authorities to seek a new investor for the project.
The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) announced on October 19 that China Merchants Port Holdings had decided not to proceed with the collaboration agreed upon in April 2023. The authority maintained that the project would continue despite the withdrawal.
In a statement, the SLPA said the decision followed an assessment of external circumstances, commercial considerations and the interests of the shareholders involved. China Merchants also informed the Hong Kong stock exchange on October 16, that terminating the project would be in the best interests of the parties.
The proposed logistics hub, covering 150,000 square metres within Colombo Port, was intended to strengthen the port’s cargo-handling and logistics infrastructure. Under the original agreement, China Merchants was to hold a 70 per cent stake in the joint venture, while the SLPA and a Sri Lankan private construction company would each own 15 per cent.
Following the Chinese company’s withdrawal, the SLPA said it was looking for a new investor to take forward the development.
Chinese investments in Sri Lanka’s strategic ports
The agreement with China Merchants, announced in 2023, represented the first major foreign investment announced after Sri Lanka’s economy collapsed in April 2022. The country experienced a severe economic crisis marked by shortages of essential goods, dwindling foreign exchange reserves and difficulties servicing its external debt. China Merchants already operates a $500 million deep-water container terminal at Colombo Port.
The Chinese company’s other significant investment is the Hambantota deep-water port on Sri Lanka’s southern coast. Developed under former pro-Chinese president Mahinda Rajapaksa, who governed the country from 2005 to 2015, the port became one of the most prominent examples of Sri Lanka’s debt-financed infrastructure expansion.
Sri Lanka borrowed heavily from China to finance infrastructure projects during Rajapaksa’s presidency. Critics have argued that some of these investments generated insufficient economic returns while increasing the country’s financial liabilities.
Unable to repay a substantial Chinese loan taken in 2017 to develop Hambantota Port, Sri Lanka handed operational control of the facility to China Merchants in exchange for $1.12 billion under a 99-year lease.
Another major Chinese-backed project is Port City Colombo, a $1.4 billion real-estate development located next to Colombo Port.
China’s expanding presence in Sri Lanka’s maritime infrastructure has raised concerns among several countries over Beijing’s growing strategic influence in the Indian Ocean and the potential implications of its access to key regional ports.
China Merchants’ withdrawal leaves the future of the $392 million logistics hub dependent on Sri Lanka’s ability to secure a new investor and sustain the project.

articles.title: Recent Developments Strengthen Port of Gothenburg RoRo Terminal - Maritime Logistics News
articles.summary: Recent Developments Strengthen Port of Gothenburg RoRo Terminal  Maritime Logistics News
articles.full_text:
Expanded terminal areas, new rail connections and modernized quays are among the investments that have strengthened Gothenburg RoRo Terminal in recent years. Traffic is also developing positively: in the first half of 2026, cargo volumes handled over the quay increased by five per cent.
Over the past three years, the terminal has undergone development. Larger, more contiguous terminal areas, additional rail tracks, new transshipment facilities and an improved ability to accommodate larger vessels are among the upgrades that have created a more modern, efficient and sustainable terminal operation.
These investments coincide with growing interest in intra-European shipping. Geopolitical uncertainty, tariff disputes and disruptions to global supply chains are prompting more companies to seek regional, predictable transport solutions with frequent connections to Europe’s major freight hubs.
Land transport in parts of Europe also faces capacity shortages and recurring disruptions. RoRo and short sea shipping can relieve pressure on heavily congested inland transport corridors and contribute to more stable, sustainable and resilient logistics flows.
Examples of completed upgrades
1. A larger, more efficient terminal area
In 2024, 144,000 square meters of new terminal space were completed in the outer port area. The expansion provided Gothenburg RoRo Terminal with a larger, more contiguous site and a more accessible operational area behind the key berths 712 and 713. The project was the port’s largest expansion since the RoRo terminal opened in the late 1970s.
2. Arken Intermodal Terminal
In 2023, Gothenburg RoRo Terminal took over the operation of Arken Intermodal Terminal, which is now an integrated part of its operations. This added 65,000 square meters of terminal space and seven rail tracks, allowing trailers to be transferred directly between trains and vessels.
3. “The Steel Tent” cross-docking facility
A building providing 11,000 square meters of space for handling steel products was constructed in 2025. The products arrive from inland locations by rail and are transferred for onward shipment to continental Europe.
4. “The Paper Roll” cross-docking facility
In 2024, the terminal invested in a 6,000-square-meter covered cross-docking facility for forest products.
5. A deeper, wider approach channel
During the 2022/2023 dredging season, the approach channel to the terminal’s quays was widened and deepened. This enables larger vessels to call and has also improved efficiency by allowing certain weather- and wind-related restrictions to be removed.
6. Larger, more modern vessels
CLdN and DFDS, the shipping lines making the most calls at the terminal, have both deployed larger, more modern vessels on their routes to and from Gothenburg.
7. Upgraded berth 710
Work to extend the quay’s projecting section and install a new ramp was completed in 2026. The upgrade enables larger vessels to use the berth and increases loading and unloading capacity.
8. Green hydrogen for heavy-duty transport
In 2024, a green hydrogen refueling station was established immediately adjacent to the terminal. Both hydrogen-powered trucks and terminal vehicles can refuel here.
9. Upgrading the eastern quay
The terminal’s eastern quay is also set to be upgraded and adapted to accommodate larger, more modern vessels.
