articles.title: Türkiye part of region with $872B infrastructure project pipeline: HSBC | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
articles.summary: Türkiye part of region with $872B infrastructure project pipeline: HSBC | Daily Sabah  Daily Sabah
articles.full_text:
Türkiye is part of a region that has an $872 billion pipeline of infrastructure projects, highlighting its investment potential and offering international and corporate investors greater exposure to the region ahead of 2030, according to a report from HSBC.
Investment in alternative logistics routes could mitigate the impact of the Iran war and make the Strait of Hormuz "redundant" in the next five years, HSBC Group CEO Georges Elhedery told an event in Dubai on Tuesday.
The report, published Monday and based on data from MEED, a Dubai-based construction industry market intelligence platform, covers the Middle East, North Africa and Türkiye (MENAT) region.
The $872 billion is part of a wider infrastructure pipeline worth $1.4 trillion.
The Iran war has shown how heavily the world relies on the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway at the mouth of the Persian Gulf between Iran and Oman. A fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade previously passed through it.
The conflict is pushing Gulf nations to channel resources into energy pipelines to ports, Elhedery said. He said this investment will help the region weather the fallout.
"Of course, we do wish and hope to see a resolution to the conflict," he said, but "Hormuz, probably in five years' time, may become redundant."
"We do see this region being able to recover and then continue growing," he said. "It will mean a lot of investment."
A recent HSBC survey of over 1,600 business leaders and around 820 global institutional investors, meanwhile, found that they still considered the Gulf an attractive investment hub.
However, after growth of 3.3% in 2025, the World Bank last week forecast a deep economic contraction of 1.3% in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region this year due to the war. That should be followed by a strong but uneven rebound in 2027.
HSBC's report doesn't say which Turkish projects are included in the $872 billion or how much of it is in Türkiye.
The country's place in the grouping reflects its role as a route between the Gulf and Europe.
The most direct example is the Development Road, a planned corridor linking the Persian Gulf to Europe through Iraq and Türkiye. It complements the Middle Corridor, the route across Central Asia and the Caucasus.
Cargo leaving Iraq's Faw Port, on the Gulf coast in Iraq's far south, would travel about 1,200 kilometers by rail to Ovaköy, a crossing on the Türkiye-Iraq border in southeastern Türkiye.
Turkish officials have linked that project to Hormuz and said that, had the Development Road been completed, the world's energy supply would have been far less affected.
Earlier this month, Türkiye opened the Çerkezköy-Kapıkule section, the longest part of the Halkalı-Kapıkule high-speed rail line, extending the network to the EU border.
The line is 229 kilometers long. It begins on Istanbul's western edge and ends at Türkiye's main rail and road border crossing with Bulgaria, at Kapıkule near the northwestern city of Edirne.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said the line is a key component of the 2,094-kilometer Turkish section of the Development Road.

articles.title: Nigeria, African Countries Push for Local Processing - Voice of Nigeria
articles.summary: Nigeria, African Countries Push for Local Processing  Voice of Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Nigeria and other African countries have called for increased local processing of raw materials to boost industrialisation, create jobs and retain more economic value within the continent.
The call was made at the Second African Raw Materials Summit 2026 in Abuja, themed “From African Feedstock to African Factories”.
Participants, including government officials, industry experts and development partners, stressed the need for stronger policies, investment, research and regional cooperation to transform Africa’s natural resources into finished products.
READ ALSO: Minister Pledges Economic Revival Through Local Processing of Raw Materials
The Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Tochukwu Udeh, said a bill proposing a minimum of 30 per cent value addition to raw materials had been returned to President Bola Tinubu for assent following a review by the Ministry of Justice and further legislative action.
Udeh said the proposed legislation was part of efforts to support the President’s ambition of growing Nigeria’s economy to one trillion dollars.
He emphasised that local processing and the commercialisation of research and innovation were critical to achieving the target.
“Because if we spend the whole of the day talking, it will still not address the challenges or proceed to action that we need to address the challenges,” the minister said, urging stakeholders to prioritise implementation.
He cited a Chinese investor who, according to him, had expressed readiness to process lithium exported from Nigeria into finished products locally.
The investor, he said, already had a battery manufacturing plant in Abia State but required coordinated support to expand the initiative.
Udeh also disclosed that the Federal Executive Council had approved the establishment of a National Research and Innovation Development Fund, with the relevant bill before the National Assembly.
To ensure that the summit produced measurable results, the minister called for a review of commitments made at the first edition, the establishment of national and continental value-addition targets, an active summit secretariat, and sustained engagement among governments, researchers, manufacturers and investors.
He proposed that the secretariat, which could be based in Nigeria, South Africa or another participating country, should monitor progress and preserve records of commitments, with the possibility of rotating its location.
Udeh also advocated regular post-summit engagement, including a dedicated communication platform, to track agreed actions.
“Please let there be no third African Raw Materials Summit if we do not collate all the things that we have said that we ought to do, all the calls to action,” he cautioned.
A Turning Point
The Director-General of the Raw Materials Research and Development Council (RMRDC), Professor Nnanyelugo Ike-Muonso, urged African countries to make the summit a turning point in the continent’s industrial development.
He said exporting unprocessed resources while importing finished products deprived Africa of jobs, wealth and opportunities for its young population.
“We dug the cobalt, but imported the batteries. We harvested 69% of world’s cocoa, but imported the chocolates. We mined the lithium, but bought back the electric vehicles, We exported our soil’s riches, and with them, we exported our jobs, our wealth, and the dreams of our youth,”Ike-Muonso said.
He proposed five action areas: a continental raw materials value-addition compact, an industrial investment pipeline, a raw materials intelligence platform, regional value chains linked to the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), and partnerships to transfer African research and technology into local industries.
The RMRDC director-general also highlighted the council’s work on locally adapted processing machinery and the Nigerian Integrated Information Statistical System for Raw Materials and Products (NISRAM), designed to map raw material deposits, processing capacity and manufacturing demand.
He urged delegates to focus on concrete industrial agreements rather than speeches and declarations.
“The world is waiting to see what Africa will do with its vast riches. And the answer must come from us, right here, right now,” he said.
The Chairman of the Senate Committee on Science and Technology, Senator Aminu Abbas, reaffirmed the National Assembly’s commitment to the proposed 30 per cent value-addition legislation.
Abbas said the bill had been returned to the legislature following observations by the Ministry of Justice, adding that lawmakers were working on it again.
He expressed hope that it would be passed within the following two to three weeks.
According to him, processing raw materials locally would create employment opportunities across manufacturing and related industries.
“You can imagine the number of employment if you process 30 percent of all our raw materials within Africa,” he said.
Abbas stressed that cooperation between the executive and legislative arms of government was essential to advancing Nigeria’s industrial development.
Stronger Research and Innovation
The United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) Representative to Nigeria and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), Ambassador Philbert Johnson, said Africa’s dependence on unprocessed raw-material exports constrained industrial development, job creation and economic diversification.
Johnson called for stronger research and innovation, reliable infrastructure, workforce development, regional trade partnerships and investment in agricultural and mineral value chains.
He also highlighted the need for resource efficiency, recycling and the use of industrial by-products and biomass in new production processes.
“The challenge before us is clear, Africa must move from exporting raw materials to producing value-added goods,” Johnson said.
He noted that UNIDO was supporting Nigeria’s industrial development through its Programme for Country Partnership, including technical assistance for agricultural and mineral value chains.
Johnson urged participants to develop practical recommendations addressing infrastructure gaps, technology constraints, financing and policy implementation.
The Director-General of the Nigerian Geological Survey Agency, Professor Olusegun Ige, called for stronger collaboration between the Ministry of Solid Minerals Development and other ministries that depend on mineral resources.
READ ALSO: RMRDC Urges Africa to Process Raw Materials Locally
Ige said reliable geological information was necessary to identify the location of raw materials and determine how best to develop them for local industries.
“Before we start the processing, we need to know where these things are. Then we need to bring them out onto the surface. Then we begin to ask for processing method,” he said.
He urged government institutions to make greater use of Nigeria’s natural resources to support local manufacturing and reduce unnecessary dependence on materials sourced from outside the country.
Sudan’s Minister of Minerals, Professor Nour Al-Daem Taha, also called for increased local mineral processing to create jobs and retain more economic value within Africa.
Taha identified local processing and refining, reliable energy supply, responsible mining practices and improved investment conditions as priorities for mineral development.
He further called for cooperation to curb mineral smuggling and strengthen training, technology transfer and workforce development.
“We need Africa to work together, to cooperate, and to share all our knowledge and business for our people and our continent,” he said.
The Sudanese minister said successful partnerships should be measured by completed projects, trained workers and opportunities created for local communities.
Participants at the summit agreed that Africa’s natural resource wealth could deliver greater economic benefits through investment, technology, infrastructure, research and consistent policies.
They also highlighted the need to strengthen regional value chains under the AfCFTA, allowing African countries to source raw materials from one another and manufacture finished products for continental and international markets.
For Nigeria, the proposed 30 per cent value-addition legislation is one of the measures aimed at advancing this objective. Its impact will depend on effective implementation, reliable energy and transport infrastructure, access to finance, industrial capacity and sustained cooperation between government and the private sector.

articles.title: Transit cargo transportation through Azerbaijan reaches record high - Apa.az
articles.summary: Transit cargo transportation through Azerbaijan reaches record high  Apa.az
articles.full_text:
Azerbaijan is expanding its role as an international transport and logistics hub. As a result of the development of the East-West and North-South international transport corridors, as well as major infrastructure projects implemented in recent years, the volume of transit cargo transportation exceeded 12 million tons in the first nine months of 2026, reaching a record high for the past five years, APA-Economics reports, citing the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport.
According to the information, this figure is 14.5% higher than in the same period last year. In particular, the volume of transit cargo transportation increased by 20.2% along the East-West route and by 19.0% along the North-South route.
Positive dynamics were also observed in port operations. In nine months of this year, container handling increased by 29% compared to the same period last year, reaching 100,000 TEU, while dry cargo handling rose by 71% to 1.73 million tons.
"The positive dynamics observed in transit transportation are the result of efforts aimed at developing transport and logistics infrastructure, digitalization, strengthening coordination among relevant institutions and thereby increasing operational efficiency, as well as expanding international cooperation. At the same time, changes in global trade routes have also contributed to growing demand for Azerbaijan's transit potential. Measures implemented in this direction have also contributed to accelerating cargo transportation along the Middle Corridor and increasing the competitiveness of the route," the ministry said.
It was noted that in recent years, several large-scale projects have been implemented to develop railway, road, maritime, and air transport infrastructure in order to increase Azerbaijan's transit capacity and competitiveness along international transport corridors.
As part of these efforts, the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars (BTK) railway line, an important component of the Middle Corridor, has been modernized, increasing its annual freight capacity to 5 million tons.
The infrastructure of the Baku International Sea Trade Port, which plays an important role in increasing the competitiveness of the Middle Corridor, has also been expanded. In recent years, the port's annual container handling capacity has increased from 100,000 TEU to 160,000 TEU. As a result of improved operational coordination, vessel handling time has been reduced from approximately 20 hours to 4–5 hours.
The port's current annual cargo handling capacity stands at 15 million tons. Under the ongoing expansion project, this figure is expected to increase to 25 million tons, while container handling capacity is planned to reach 500,000 TEU.

articles.title: Egypt’s economy better equipped to absorb disruptions - Al Majalla
articles.summary: Egypt’s economy better equipped to absorb disruptions  Al Majalla
articles.full_text:
Record remittances, stronger investment inflows and higher foreign reserves are giving Egypt’s economy greater room to absorb shocks, but sustaining the recovery will depend on addressing financial imbalances and accelerating economic reforms.
Egypt found itself better equipped to absorb disruptions caused by the latest regional turmoil than it was four years ago, when the Russia-Ukraine war exposed deep-seated distortions in the foreign exchange market and triggered a severe dollar shortage. Performance in the 2025/2026 fiscal year points to a shift in how the country manages external pressures, but it does not mean that the economy has overcome its structural weaknesses.
Real GDP growth accelerated to 5.1%, alongside stronger foreign currency inflows and rising investment. Remittances from Egyptians working abroad, together with tourism revenues and foreign direct investment, helped bolster the country’s foreign currency resources. Foreign reserves also reached $57.3bn in September 2026, providing a larger buffer against volatility and helping Egypt meet its external obligations.
Egypt welcomed around 19 million tourists in 2025, while authorities are banking on tourism revenues exceeding $20bn in 2026, despite regional tensions. The Suez Canal, meanwhile, remains well below its record levels, even though revenues rose to $4.67bn in the 2025/2026 fiscal year, up 23% from the previous year.
Revenues reached around $10.25bn in 2023 before Houthi attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea, which began in late 2023, disrupted navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait and prompted international shipping companies to reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid security risks. These disruptions reduced canal traffic and revenues, depriving Egypt of a significant source of foreign currency at a time when the country was seeking to strengthen its dollar reserves and ease pressure on its balance of payments.

articles.title: Kenyan cult leader convicted in deaths of 190 children - TimesLIVE
articles.summary: Kenyan cult leader convicted in deaths of 190 children  TimesLIVEShakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya  BBCKenyan cult leader guilty on all charges over 191 starvation deaths  eNCAKenyan cult leader found guilty over 190 children starved to death in the hope of ‘meeting Jesus’  CNNToday in Africa — October 19, 2026: Kenyan Starvation Cult Leader Convicted of Murder, Samora Machel Remembered 40 Years After His Death&nbsp...
articles.full_text:
A Kenyan court on Monday found starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.
Mackenzie and his co-accused will be given their sentence on November 6.
He was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.
Prosecutors say Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola Forest. Many were severely decomposed, with only 26 bodies able to be identified.
Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are ongoing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, who is one of the co-accused.
When his name was read out by the judge he stood silently.
Family members of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa High Court.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.
Speaking before the verdict, he told Reuters: “It has been really a heavy thing (for) us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems, I was hoping for this particular day.”
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola Forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenyan President William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.
People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.
A former taxi driver, Mackenzie forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, branding such institutions as Satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names like Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told police that his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police arrested him again in April 2023 and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.
Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, which lies about 30km from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

articles.title: The West’s transactional pivot to India - GIS Reports
articles.summary: The West’s transactional pivot to India  GIS Reports
articles.full_text:
The West is courting India for trade, minerals, technology and defense – and, above all, to break China’s grip on supply chains.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
- The EU’s new FTA with India is a geoeconomic tool binding them together
- U.S. broadens its security approach with India into major commercial ties
- De-risking with India is slow, with full political alignment unlikely
While the United States and the European Union have traditionally approached India through largely distinct prisms – Washington through a security-centric lens and Brussels with a regulatory-trade focus – the core objective of both strategies is practically identical. The Western powers are engaged in a sophisticated, albeit sometimes clumsy, campaign to court India to secure critical minerals, high-tech manufacturing partnerships and supply chain alternatives. This is less a geopolitical love affair and more a transactional necessity driven by the realization that the West cannot reduce its dependence on China by itself; it needs India and other middle powers.
India is particularly attractive to the West because of the size and growth of its economy, its large industrial and technological base, substantial labor force and capability in becoming both a major supplier and end-market. Although the European and American approaches differ in emphasis, both are attempting to persuade India that deeper economic integration with the West can serve India’s interests as well as their own.
The EU’s regulatory and trade approach
Brussels has made the clearest trade-led effort to cultivate India. In January 2026, the EU and India concluded negotiations on a landmark free trade agreement (FTA) after years of difficult talks. The two sides plan to sign it in December 2026 and to bring it into force in early 2027. The European Commission called it the largest trade agreement either side has ever concluded. India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96.6 percent of EU goods exports by value.
Yet the agreement’s significance goes beyond tariff cuts. Bilateral trade totaled 192 billion euros in 2025, and the EU is India’s third-largest trading partner. The bloc’s foreign direct investment stock in India reached 132 billion euros in 2024, making the EU the country’s leading foreign investor. The FTA therefore seeks to move an already substantial relationship toward deeper economic integration.
The EU’s economic-security strategy increasingly treats trade policy as a tool for building strategic resilience. The goal is not simply to sell more European goods and services in India, but also to build more diversified production networks. The European and Indian economies are complementary: Europe has sophisticated industrial technology, capital and high-value manufacturing capabilities, while India offers a large domestic market, a growing manufacturing base, engineering expertise and a vast pool of skilled workers.
Even so, one point of disagreement reveals underlying tensions. New Delhi views Europe’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) with deep suspicion. The mechanism imposes a carbon charge on imports of carbon-intensive goods such as steel and aluminum. Indian negotiators see CBAM as protectionism dressed in green clothing, a direct threat to India’s nascent industrial base.
The FTA does not exempt India from CBAM, and the EU has said India will receive no more favorable CBAM treatment than any other country. However, the EU has offered technical assistance to help Indian industries decarbonize, effectively offering financial aid to help their steelmakers meet European standards. The EU is using its regulatory power, backed by the promise of market access, to reshape India’s industrial policy.
Brussels’ critical minerals ambitions
The EU’s most pressing resource need is securing raw materials for the energy transition without deepening its dependence on China, which dominates processing of most critical minerals. Individual member states have signed their own critical minerals agreements with New Delhi: Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with Italy and the Netherlands, and a Joint Declaration of Intent with Germany. They cover exploration, processing, recycling and supply-chain resilience.
India’s critical-mineral potential is real but unproven. In 2023, the Geological Survey of India reported 5.9 million metric tons of inferred lithium-bearing ore in Jammu and Kashmir, its first major lithium find. India also holds licenses to explore Indian Ocean seabed nodules containing nickel, copper and cobalt. Developing these will take years of investment in exploration, extraction and processing, where Europe could help with technology and finance. In return, the EU might seek long-term supply agreements.
The EU is also backing a proposed “Critical Minerals Club” to set common standards for responsible mining and processing. Helping India build a sustainable mining sector would give Europe an alternative supply chain less exposed to China: capital and technology today in exchange for secure raw-material flows tomorrow.
Europe’s semiconductor gambit
Beyond minerals, Europe is looking to India for high-tech resilience. The European Chips Act aims to double the EU’s share of the global semiconductor market by 2030. However, Europe lacks the fabrication capacity and skilled workforce to reach that target on its own. The EU has therefore turned to India, whose semiconductor mission has moved into a second phase with an approved budget of about $13 billion.
In early 2023, the EU launched a Trade and Technology Council (TTC) with India, its second such forum after the one it set up with the U.S. In November 2023, under the TTC, the two sides signed an MoU on semiconductor ecosystems, supply chains and innovation. At the 2025 TTC meeting, the EU and India discussed cooperation on semiconductors, solar technology, pharmaceuticals, critical technologies and other strategic sectors. Such cooperation serves a dual purpose for Europe: It reduces the continent’s reliance on Chinese-made chips for automobiles and, by training Indian engineers to European standards, binds India more closely to Europe’s technological ecosystem.
Washington’s turn to trade
Washington’s relationship with New Delhi has traditionally been shaped by strategic and security considerations, particularly through defense cooperation in the form of the Quad, broader Indo-Pacific security and technology partnerships. Nevertheless, the economic dimension has grown in importance. In February 2025, the U.S. and India announced Mission 500, which aims to more than double bilateral trade to $500 billion by 2030. They also opened negotiations on a bilateral trade agreement intended to improve market access, reduce tariff and nontariff barriers and integrate the two economies more closely.
Since then, the path has been turbulent. After imposing 50 percent tariffs on Indian goods in August 2025, partly over India’s purchases of Russian oil, Washington agreed in February 2026 to cut them to 18 percent under an interim trade framework. Later that month, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the tariffs. Most Indian exports now face a 10 percent duty, and the interim deal remains unsigned.
The negotiations reflect both opportunity and tension. America has long complained that India’s tariff regime and regulatory barriers make it harder for U.S. companies to access the Indian market than for Indian firms to enter the American market. Washington’s negotiators have therefore approached India not only as a geopolitical partner but also as a commercial counterpart whose market they want to open further to American exporters.
America’s critical minerals push
Critical minerals provide a particularly clear bridge between the security and economic dimensions of the U.S.-India relationship. In May 2026, the two countries established a Strategic Critical Minerals Cooperation Framework to deepen cooperation in mining, processing, recycling and financing.
New Delhi is seeking to reduce vulnerabilities in strategic raw materials while developing domestic exploration, processing and recycling capacity. The U.S. Department of Commerce notes that India has allocated significant public resources to developing its critical-minerals sector and has identified substantial opportunities to use American mining equipment, services, technology and investment.
Thus, the U.S. objective is not simply to extract Indian minerals. A more sustainable model would involve U.S. capital and technology helping India build domestic value chains, with Indian firms subsequently integrating into wider American production networks.

Economic weight, diplomatic independence
A broader political calculation underpins this Western economic courtship. India is increasingly important in global economic governance and is one of the few countries with enough economic weight to shape international supply chains while maintaining considerable diplomatic independence. As a result, the EU and the U.S. have expanded cooperation with India across trade, technology, connectivity, defense and global governance. In 2025, European and Indian officials discussed mutual economic security, resilient supply chains, trade and investment, infrastructure connectivity, the EU’s Global Gateway and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor.
